title: ISO 216 A-series paper sizes: the square-root-of-two ratio, A0–A6 dimensions and the history of DIN 476

facts.text: In the ISO A series, the long side of every sheet is the square root of two, about 1.4142 or 1.414, times its short side.
If a sheet with this ratio is cut into two equal pieces parallel to its shorter side, each piece has the same ratio as the original sheet.
Because of the square-root-of-two ratio, width and height cannot both be round metric lengths, so the system fixes the area instead: A0 has an area of one square meter.
A0 measures 841 by 1189 millimeters (1,189 mm), which is 0.999949 square meters, or about one square meter.
Each A size is half of the one before it: A1 is half of A0, A2 a quarter, A3 an eighth, A4 one sixteenth, A5 1/32 and A6 1/64 of a square meter.

The millimeter sizes in the standard were found by halving the larger size again and again, each time rounding down to a whole millimeter, so two sheets of the next size together are never larger than the sheet they came from.
Halving 1189 gives 594.5, rounded down to 594 for A1; halving 841 gives 420.5, rounded down to 420 for A2; halving 297 gives 148.5, rounded down to 148 for A5.
facts.note: 由 s1 的尺寸表與「逐次減半、無條件捨去到整數公釐」的規則推得

facts.text: The short sides of A3 (297), A4 (210) and A6 (105) are exactly half of the long side of the next larger size (594, 420 and 210 millimeters).
facts.note: 由 s1 的尺寸表推得

facts.text: Typical office and laser printer paper weighs 80 g per square meter, so one A4 sheet of it weighs 5 g.
With 80 g per square meter paper, an A0 sheet weighs about 80 g, A1 40 g, A2 20 g, A3 10 g and A4 5 g.
facts.note: 由 s1 的 80 g/m² 與各尺寸面積推得

facts.text: To copy two facing A4 pages of a journal onto one A4 sheet, a copier is set to 71 percent, the square root of one half, and no paper margin is wasted.

On 25 October 1786, Georg Christoph Lichtenberg, a physics professor at the University of Göttingen, explained the advantages of the square-root-of-two ratio in a letter and noted that paper of that shape was commonly available.
On 3 November 1798, a French law on taxing paper defined several formats that match modern ISO sizes exactly, but this French series soon fell out of use and was forgotten.
More than a hundred years later, Dr. Walter Porstmann independently reinvented the A, B and C series in Germany.
In 1922 Porstmann’s formats became the German standard DIN 476, replacing a wide variety of earlier paper sizes to make stocking paper and copying documents cheaper and more efficient.
Other countries soon adopted the system as a national standard, including Belgium in 1924, the Netherlands in 1925, Japan in 1951, the United Kingdom in 1959 and Australia in 1974.
In 1975 the series became the international standard ISO 216 and the official format for United Nations documents.
Today the A series is used in almost every country except in North America; the United States and Canada mainly use other formats.
US Letter paper measures 216 by 279 millimeters.
US paper formats alternate between two ratios, 17/11 (about 1.545) and 22/17 (about 1.294), so reducing or enlarging one US format to the next leaves an empty margin.
